doc.title: Sheila Jordan interviewed by Monk Rowe, Middleburgh, New York, May 11, 2002

title: Beaten up outside her New York loft
summary: In New York, after a session at her loft, she was attacked by four men while with two painter friends and rescued by a plainclothes policeman.

story.theme_name: Gangsters, bootleggers and rough clubs of Prohibition

He’s waiting to get your reaction and if you flip out they’ll put you for assaulting an officer or whatever, you know? So I said, “Oh, gosh,” I said, “boy that’s strong,” or something like that I said. Well I said, “I’m not going to be staying in Detroit anyway.” I said, “I’m going to New York.” Well I was chasing Bird you know. So he said, “Oh we’re so cosmopolitan.” You know? And I didn’t say anything. All of a sudden some little voice that takes care of me said, “Shut up. Don’t say anything. They’re waiting.” I came to New York and I was walking on my street, I was having these sessions in my loft like you wouldn’t believe. Everybody showed up there. Sonny Rollins, everybody came to my loft. Monk, everybody. Naturally Bird was always there. There’s a session going full bloom, a lot of the kids that were studying with Lennie Tristano and going like this, I think Warne Marsh was up there that night playing. I went out with two young black painters, artists, to get some food. On my way back four guys, white guys, jumped out of the bar on the corner where I lived and held the guys and threw me down and started beating me up, actually knocked one of my teeth out. And all of a sudden I looked up and I saw this guy in this tweed overcoat, and he had a gun drawn. And I said oh my God, here I left Detroit to come to New York to get away from this and now I’m going to get murdered. Here he’s going to kill me. You know? For being with black friends, which I don’t even think about. He was a plain clothesman. And he saved my life. [clock] These guys were kicking me like you wouldn’t believe. He comes over and he says, “Do you know this woman? Is she related to you?” “No, officer.” He of course showed his badge, because he was a plain clothesman. So then he took them aside and then he took me and he said, “What do you want to do about this? Do you want to press charges?” And I said, “Yeah.” He said, “I’m going to tell you something. They know where you live, so you do what you want.” He said, “I’ll do anything you want me to do.” So I talked to the two guys that I was with, the two painters, and they said, “Sheila, let it go.” Sometimes I wonder, did I do the right thing?
I don’t know if I ever did the right thing you know. I thought oh they need to be punished.

But there’s self-preservation you have to consider. SJ; There was. And they did know where I lived. And they actually weren’t even from the neighborhood they just happened to be passing through. But how is that for a story? Isn’t that bizarre?
